author_note.title: A shawl, and the questions it opened
paragraphs: This book began at a dinner table.

At a dinner party with friends, I noticed the cloth used for the table mats and hand towels. My host also had shawls for sale, and I bought one. I fell in love with it. Perhaps I had seen something like it before, but I had never paused to understand where it came from or whose work I was looking at.

I was already working on Project Odisha, exploring the places, culture and literature of Odisha. This encounter gave that work a personal direction. I wanted to learn about the people behind the cloth, the place they called home and the lives around its making.

The reading took me far beyond the shawl. Information was scattered across reports, studies and individual accounts. Over the following weeks, I read and brought these stories together, trying to keep people at the centre: those who grow food, keep seeds, embroider, teach, learn and sing.

My delight in the designs found other forms, too. I made a bag inspired by them and had ten T-shirts printed. Those were my own adaptations. As my curiosity grew, I wanted to understand more of the lives and work from which that inspiration came.

I felt embarrassed by how little I had known about this part of Odisha. That feeling soon became a reason to keep learning. What had first caught my eye as a beautiful garment had opened questions about skill, livelihood, land, memory and belonging.
I have not yet visited Niyamgiri. This first book grows from weeks of reading and research; the visit, and the listening I hope to do there, still lie ahead. There is much I do not yet know.
I hope these pages bring you insight and some of the joy this discovery has brought me. I hope, too, that when you look at a cloth, you pause a little longer with the people whose work gives it life.
For me, this is a beginning.
Ahimanikya Satapathy

preface.title: Before we begin
paragraphs: “He created fruit in the hills, grains in the plains,”
— Dambu Praska, Dongria Kondh singer. English rendering published by Living Farms, 2009.

In his song of Niyam Raja, Praska names the food that sustains life. We begin with the hills and the people who make their homes there, then follow the work of growing food and taking a harvest to market. Cloth and ornaments bring makers and wearers into the story. Students, teachers and singers carry us towards questions of language, memory and what one generation shares with another. Each account belongs to particular people, places and years.

This book brings together published research and attributed reporting. It cannot supply every voice or resolve every uncertainty. The notes keep those limits visible. Photographs and imagined illustrations offer different kinds of pause; the picture notes at the back identify each one.
Read slowly enough to notice who is speaking, who is doing the work and who is making the decision. Let the names stay with the cloth, the crop and the song.

closing.title: Looking again
paragraphs: I began with a shawl. The reading brought me to people whose names I now want to remember.

Site Jakesika’s embroidery, Mukteswar Wadaka’s teaching and the work of keeping seeds in circulation belong to different lives. Bringing them into one book does not make those lives the same. Each asks for its own attention.

The cloth that first delighted me still does. But I look at it differently now. Alongside colour and pattern, I think about time: the hours spent making, the work fitted around other work, and the knowledge passed between people. Beauty has become a reason to pay closer attention.
There is much more to learn. I hope to keep asking, listening and revising what I think I know.
If this book leaves you curious, I hope you follow that curiosity towards the people and their work. Remember a name. Look again at a familiar object. Ask where it came from and how it was made.
I bought a shawl that evening. I am still learning how much there is to see in it.

glossary.definition: The roots used as a dye material in NIFT’s account of Kotpad yarn colouring.
glossary.editorial_limit: Do not add a botanical species identification; source wording is roots.

glossary.definition: A priestess; the seed accounts describe particular bejuni helping recover varieties and conducting rituals before sowing.
glossary.editorial_limit: Do not generalise one account into every village’s practice.

glossary.definition: A seed festival described in the 2018 reporting, with seeds prepared and brought to a priestess before planting.
Dongria Kondh Development Agency; the development agency referred to in the training and livelihood accounts.
glossary.editorial_limit: Expansion also in Sahapedia’s work account; source printed p.24.

glossary.definition: Geographical indication: an indication linking goods to a place whose origin gives them a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic.
glossary.editorial_limit: A definition, not proof that an individual depicted cloth is GI-certified.

glossary.definition: A village assembly. In the Niyamgiri case, the assemblies examined community, cultural and religious claims connected with the proposed mining.
glossary.editorial_limit: Reuse the chapter’s verified 18 April 2013 judgment, paragraphs 55–62; not a current permissions guide.

glossary.definition: Used here in the title Jatapu (Kuvi) Primer and for Prasanna Sree’s devised script. The primer uses Telugu-based writing, not that devised script.
glossary.editorial_limit: Pair with chapter sources for devised script; not a name for every Kuvi-speaking community.

glossary.definition: Cloth embroidered by Dongria makers, worn and given as well as made for sale; sources also spell it Kapdagonda or Kapdaganda.
A blade-shaped hair ornament also used to cut thread and trim loose ends in the embroidery account.
glossary.editorial_limit: Not a universal name assigned to every visible hairpin.

glossary.definition: A town in Koraput district and the name associated here with its cotton dyeing and handloom-weaving tradition, distinct from Kapadaganda embroidery.
A Dravidian language closely related to Kuvi, with a separate entry in the Central Institute of Indian Languages collections.
A Dravidian language spoken in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. Its name is not interchangeable with Kui; Kuwi is a spelling used in one primer’s title.
National Institute of Fashion Technology, publisher of the Kapilo Mahanta craft profile used in the Kotpad chapter.
The deity associated with the Niyamgiri hills in the worship, seed and song accounts.
glossary.editorial_limit: No newly invented translated epithet or universal creed.

glossary.definition: Odisha Rural Development and Marketing Society, the state organisation referred to in the account of product marketing plans.
A building whose walls and roof use durable materials, such as burnt brick, stone, cement or concrete.
glossary.editorial_limit: A materials-based category, not a claim that a house is better suited to every household.
